smm_pool.title: First Impression Ads
smm_pool.text: This could end badly… A few weeks ago, Meta announced the test of a feature in the US called First Impression Ads . This allows advertisers to book the first ad people see in their feeds. Understand that this isn’t some new ad unit that will look any different or a new placement. It’s not new inventory at all. And that could be a problem. Why I’m Concerned This is simply giving advertisers the option to reserve the first ad spot in the feed that was otherwise available to everyone. I worry about the impact this may have. Presumably, this first impression is effective, and it would surely cost more. If it’s not any more effective, then there wouldn’t be a reason to reserve it. If it truly is more effective, it will be in high demand. So let’s assume that the biggest brands then eat up that first impression slot. That removes it from distribution for the rest of advertisers with small and medium-sized budgets. And if that first impression is then rarely available for these other brands, what will it do to results? They’d get worse, right? It all depends on how much results depend on that first impression slot now, and how available that slot becomes when this feature rolls out (assuming it moves beyond a test). Will It Move Beyond a Test? First Impression Ads could be an example of Meta profiting from demand for a select few, while hurting the product for the rest. Or maybe I’m missing something, but it seems like a terrible idea. Stay tuned while we wait to see what happens with this initial test. It’s the step-by-step system for reviewing, editing, and approving content before it goes live, covering stages from drafting through final sign-off. Why do approval workflows fail? People share product recommendations in Instagram Stories, leave feedback in TikTok comments, and (sadly) most of those posts never tag you. That’s where social listening comes in — it shows you what people say about you, your competitors, and your industry when you’re not looking. Social media monitoring tracks what people say to you (tags, mentions, DMs). Social listening looks at what they say about you and why. The main benefits of social listening are deeper audience insight, faster reputation management, earlier trend spotting, better product decisions, and sharper competitive positioning. A workable social listening strategy has five steps: set goals, mine your own comments, pick your keywords, choose tools, and turn the data into decisions.
